title: Cloud vendor inference battle notes
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact, tactical battlecard for GTM and SEs comparing Redwood Inference (runtime + platform) to the three dominant cloud managed inference offerings (AWS, GCP, Microsoft/Azure). Focus is on real objections we hear in RTCs, concise win themes, technical hooks SEs can use, and recommended plays for SMB / mid-market / enterprise buyers.

TL;DR (one-liners to use in sales conversations):
- For product teams who measure success by predictable latency, cost-per-inference, and rollout safety, Redwood offers a unified runtime and ops surface that reduces surprise costs and operational toil compared to cloud-managed endpoints.
- Cloud vendors give scale and ecosystem but leave performance tuning, batch/cache design, and cross-environment consistency as buyer responsibilities — that’s where Redwood adds immediate value.

Quick competitor profiles (high level):
- AWS (SageMaker Endpoints / Bedrock / model infra): integrated with AWS infra, broad feature set, good for teams already committed to AWS. Strength: turnkey autoscaling, IAM, marketplace models. Weakness: limited cross-cloud/private parity; customers report opaque per-request economics and heavy engineering work to replicate advanced KV caching / batching.
- GCP (Vertex AI / Matching Engine): strong data/ML workflow integrations and good UX for Google shops. Strength: pipeline + data integration. Weakness: managed endpoint ergonomics focused on standard ML workloads, not high-throughput LLM serving optimizations (cache + KV, kernel selection).
- Azure (Azure OpenAI + Azure ML endpoints): convenience for Microsoft ecosystem and enterprise contracts. Strength: enterprise agreements, compliance integrations. Weakness: usage model often locked to vendor model variants and fewer knobs for reducing token-level unit economics or graceful fallbacks between model variants.

Where cloud vendors win (be honest):
- Deep integration with their cloud provider (IAM, VPCs, identity, billing).
- Broad marketplace and first-party models (useful for simple, low-ops proof-of-concepts).
- Enterprise contracting and audit/logging baked into their platform for some compliance regimes.

Where Redwood wins (core battle themes):
1) Unified inference surface across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments
   - Messaging: "Same API, same rollout primitives, same observability whether you run on Redwood-hosted or in your VPC/on-prem" — counteracts vendor lock-in arguments.
2) Production-first performance controls
   - Messaging: "We provide batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization recommendations out-of-the-box so token cost and tail latency become controllable knobs, not surprises."
3) Transparent economics and per-token cost tooling
   - Messaging: "Token-level cost and latency breakdowns enable developers and finance to forecast spend and spot regressions quickly."
4) Smart routing & graceful degradation
   - Messaging: "Router policies let you route by latency, cost, or region and automatically fallback to cheaper model variants when capacity is constrained."
5) Observability + safe rollouts
   - Messaging: "Built-in rollouts, A/B, canary and automatic fallback reduce both engineering effort and customer risk during model upgrades."

Technical differentiators to call out in SE conversations (concise):
- Kernel selection and sequence-length aware compilation: faster inference on mixed sequence workloads vs generic managed endpoints.
- Continuous batching and KV cache primitives exposed as first-class controls (not afterthought).
- Quantization recommendations by workload and automated suggestion engine (Optimize) to trade latency vs quality.
- Prefix caching for assistant-style applications that dramatically reduces token cost for repeated system/preamble tokens.

Common buyer personas and pain points to map to (tailor the pitch):
- ML Platform Lead (enterprise): "I need predictable costs and a migration path off experimental infra." → emphasize SLA, Dedicated, and private-control-plane options.
- Product engineering lead (startup): "I want fast time-to-value and low latency for chat." → emphasize hosted API, streaming, function/tool calling, and quick perf wins from caching.
- Security/compliance buyer: "We must keep data in our VPC/HSM and have audit logs." → emphasize Private deployment, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit traceability.

Discovery questions for reps/SEs (to surface Redwood advantages):
- What does your current tail latency look like at p95/p99 for conversational flows longer than 2k tokens?
- How do you track token-level spend across routes/models today?
- Do you have any existing KV/prefix caching strategy? If not, how often do you repeat system messages or domain prompts?
- What is your rollout process when you change model versions? Do you have automatic fallback on quality or latency regressions?
- Are you planning to run inference across multiple clouds or need an on-prem option?

Objections and suggested responses:
- "We’re already on AWS/GCP/Azure — why add Redwood?" → "Redwood sits on top of cloud infra or can run privately. The value is consistent performance, cost predictability, and rollout tooling you don’t get out-of-the-box — we reduce both engineering lift and unit economics."
- "Cloud managed endpoints are cheaper because they’re native." → "Sticker price for compute may look low but missing features (cache, batching, smart routing) drive up per-token realized cost. We can run a short pilot with cost/latency baselines to quantify delta within 2–4 weeks."
- "We’re worried about lock-in." → "Redwood’s API and model catalog let you run the same workload on-hosted, dedicated reserved pools, or in your VPC — simplifying migrations and hybrid setups."

Pricing / economics talking points (examples you can customize):
- Positioning: "We don’t promise to always be cheapest on raw GPU hours, we promise better unit economics for production LLM features because of platform-level efficiencies (caching, batching, optimized kernels)."
- Offer pilot pricing: 2–4 week evaluation with usage credits + observability enabled so customers can see token-level savings and latency improvements.

Competitive plays by segment (recommended):
- Startup / SMB: quick-hosted pilot (managed onboarding + sample prompt set) focusing on latency/UX wins; emphasize low-touch integration and streaming.
- Mid-market: propose Dedicated reserved pool trial for stable throughput and show cost-per-1000-token comparisons vs their current managed endpoint usage.
- Enterprise: position Private deployment with compliance add-ons and a migration path from native cloud endpoints; highlight rollouts, audit logs, and dedicated support.

Deal-level tactics / proof points to bring:
- Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 improvements on typical assistant workloads (8k context, 2–8 concurrent users per GPU) versus vendor-managed endpoints (numbers from internal bench runs).
- Customer references: anonymized notes from customers who reduced token spend by X% after enabling prefix caching and smart batching.
- Live demo scripts: 10–15 minute demo showing same prompt hitting two backends (cloud-managed vs Redwood) with live token-cost telemetry and rollout control flip.

Next steps for GTM (actionable):
- Create a 2-week pilot kit (playbook, sample prompts, permission checklist, dashboards) for SEs to run with prospects.
- Produce one-pager with head-to-head operational differences (runtime features, rollout, private deployment) and include simple cost comparison worksheet.
- Collect three anonymized customer metrics to use as proof: % token savings from caching, p95 latency delta, time-to-recover from model regression with rollbacks.

Appendix: quick snippets to use in collateral or sales emails
- "Reduce token surprises — Redwood shows you per-token cost and where it comes from so engineering and finance stop having surprise invoices."
- "Run the same inference tooling in-hosted, in your VPC, or on-prem — one API, fewer migrations."
- "We optimize both kernels and deployment policies so your assistant is faster and cheaper without changing model behavior."

(End of notes)
